overview:
In Jain thought, the tension between “evidence” and “interpretation” is handled through a sophisticated epistemological framework that refuses both naïve objectivism and arbitrary relativism. Evidence, in the Jain sense, is not merely raw data from the senses or scripture; it is valid cognition (pramāṇa) that has passed tests of reliability, coherence, and ethical alignment. Interpretation, correspondingly, is articulated through standpoints (naya) and the doctrine of conditional predication (syādvāda), which insist that every claim about reality is partial, context-bound, and open to further qualification. Together, pramāṇa and naya form a paired structure: evidence aims at comprehensive grasp, interpretation at perspectival articulation.

Classical Jain epistemology, as systematized in texts like the Tattvārthasūtra, distinguishes between indirect knowledge (parokṣa) and direct knowledge (aparokṣa or pratyakṣa). Sensory and scriptural knowledge (mati-jñāna and śruta-jñāna) are indirect, mediated by organs, language, and inference; clairvoyance, telepathy, and omniscience (avadhi, manaḥparyāya, kevala-jñāna) are direct, arising from the soul’s own unobstructed capacity. Evidence, therefore, is graded: what the senses and scriptures report is provisionally valid, but subject to correction by higher, less obstructed forms of knowing. Interpretation enters when finite knowers, operating with indirect cognition, attempt to describe an infinitely complex reality composed of substances (dravya), attributes (guṇa), and modes (paryāya). Anekāntavāda—the doctrine of non-one-sidedness—states that no single finite statement can exhaust such complexity.

The naya theory explains how interpretation works without collapsing into mere opinion. Each naya is a legitimate standpoint that highlights certain aspects of a thing while bracketing others. For example, a substance can be described from the standpoint of its permanence, its momentary modes, its practical function, or its logical definition. None of these descriptions is simply “wrong”; each is evidentially grounded yet incomplete. Syādvāda then provides the linguistic discipline for expressing this structure: statements are framed conditionally—“in some respect, it is”; “in some respect, it is not”; “in some respect, it is indescribable”—to mark the limits of one’s evidence and the partiality of one’s interpretation. Evidence and interpretation thus interlock: evidence constrains which standpoints are admissible, while interpretation acknowledges that any evidential claim is situated.

This framework has important implications for how Jains read their own scriptures and engage with other traditions. Scriptural testimony (śruta) is recognized as a powerful but indirect source of evidence: it preserves the insights of omniscient beings and accomplished teachers, yet it reaches ordinary listeners through language, memory, and commentary. As Samayasāra and other texts emphasize, scripture itself is not identical with knowledge; it is a vehicle that must be understood, tested, and integrated with one’s own experiential and ethical practice. Interpretation of scriptural passages therefore requires attention to context, genre, and the spiritual maturity of both speaker and listener. Anekāntavāda encourages respectful dialogue with non-Jain philosophies by treating their doctrines as partial standpoints rather than sheer error, while still allowing rigorous critique when claims overreach their evidential basis.

In modern application, “evidence versus interpretation” becomes especially salient when Jains confront scientific findings, historical criticism of texts, or ethical dilemmas in technology, ecology, and social life. The Jain model does not ask practitioners to reject empirical science; instead, it invites them to see scientific results as one powerful naya—grounded in sensory and inferential pramāṇa—alongside ethical and spiritual standpoints that consider non-violence (ahiṃsā), interdependence, and karmic consequences. Disagreements are often traced not to a lack of evidence but to differing standpoints and unacknowledged assumptions. The discipline of syādvāda can help prevent dogmatic claims that go beyond available evidence, while the aspiration toward kevala-jñāna reminds practitioners that all finite interpretations are provisional. In this way, Jain epistemology offers a nuanced account of how evidence should guide interpretation, and how interpretation must continually confess its limits before the many-sidedness of reality.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (Digambara and Śvetāmbara lineages)
primary_sources.translation: By means of pramāṇa and naya, the various objects are understood as possessing non-one-sided (anekānta) nature.
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārthasūtra is a foundational Sanskrit compendium of Jain doctrine, accepted across major Jain traditions. In its discussions of knowledge, it distinguishes pramāṇa (valid cognition) from naya (standpoints), thereby structurally separating evidential grasp from interpretive perspective. Later commentaries elaborate that pramāṇa aims at comprehensive understanding, while naya expresses partial views conditioned by practical or logical aims. This verse encapsulates how evidence (pramāṇa) and interpretation (naya) jointly disclose the many-sidedness of reality.

primary_sources.title: Aptamīmāṃsā
primary_sources.author: Samantabhadra
primary_sources.original_text:
एकान्तनिश्चयो मोहात्, नान्यथाव्यवहारतः।
स्यान्नयैः परतत्त्वस्य, बोधोऽनेकान्तलक्षणः॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ekānta-niścayo mohāt, nānyathā-vyavahārataḥ;
syān-nayaiḥ para-tattvasya, bodho ’nekānta-lakṣaṇaḥ
primary_sources.translation: Dogmatic certainty (ekānta-niścaya) arises from delusion, not from proper practical engagement. Through conditional standpoints (syān-naya), the highest reality is known as marked by non-one-sidedness.
primary_sources.notes: Samantabhadra’s Aptamīmāṃsā is a key Sanskrit treatise defending Jain epistemology against rival schools. Here he criticizes absolute, one-sided assertions that ignore the limits of evidence and the role of standpoint. The verse explicitly links delusive dogmatism to misuse of interpretation, and presents syādvāda and naya as disciplined modes of interpretation that respect the many-sided nature of reality. Evidence is not denied; rather, it is protected from distortion by acknowledging its perspectival expression.

primary_sources.title: Samayasāra
primary_sources.author: Kundakunda
primary_sources.original_text:
ण णाणं सुत्तं, सुत्तं तु णाणं न होइ।
णाणं तु सुत्तस्स, भावो णिच्चो उवायो॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ṇa ṇāṇaṃ suttaṃ, suttaṃ tu ṇāṇaṃ na hoi;
ṇāṇaṃ tu suttassa, bhāvo ṇicco uvāyo
primary_sources.translation: Scripture (sutta) is not itself knowledge (jñāna), nor does knowledge consist merely in scripture. Rather, knowledge is the enduring inner state for which scripture is a means.
primary_sources.notes: Samayasāra, composed in Prakrit, is a central Digambara text on the nature of the soul and right knowledge. This passage underscores the distinction between evidential cognition and its linguistic or textual vehicle. Scripture provides interpretive guidance and preserves teachings, but it is not identical with knowledge; it must be internalized and verified in experience. The verse is frequently cited to caution against confusing textual authority with direct evidence, and to highlight the interpretive work required to move from scriptural words to lived understanding.

primary_sources.title: Anekāntajayapatākā
primary_sources.author: Haribhadra Sūri
primary_sources.original_text:
नैकान्तो नाप्यनैकान्तो, नायोऽयं तत्त्वदर्शिनाम्।
प्रमाणैः परिसंयुक्तो, नयः स्याद् अर्थगोचरे॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
naikānto nāpy anekānto, nāyo ’yaṃ tattva-darśinām;
pramāṇaiḥ parisaṃyukto, nayaḥ syād artha-gocare
primary_sources.translation: Neither sheer absolutism nor sheer indeterminacy is the standpoint of those who see reality. A standpoint (naya), joined with pramāṇas, properly concerns an object.
primary_sources.notes: Haribhadra, a major Śvetāmbara philosopher, wrote extensively on anekāntavāda and comparative philosophy. In this verse he clarifies that naya is not a license for arbitrary interpretation: it must be coordinated with pramāṇa. Evidence and interpretation are thus mutually regulating—standpoints must be grounded in valid cognition, and pramāṇas are expressed through appropriately qualified standpoints. The text is often used to explain how Jain thinkers avoid both rigid dogmatism and chaotic relativism.

misconceptions.myth: Evidence in Jainism is purely scriptural, and interpretation is simply obedience to traditional authority.
misconceptions.reality: Jain epistemology treats scriptural testimony (śruta) as one important but indirect form of evidence, alongside sensory perception, inference, and higher cognitive states like clairvoyance and omniscience. Scripture must be understood, tested, and integrated with experience and ethical practice; it is not identical with knowledge. Interpretation involves disciplined use of standpoints (naya) and conditional predication (syādvāda), not mere repetition of inherited views.

misconceptions.myth: Anekāntavāda means that all interpretations are equally true, so evidence no longer matters.
misconceptions.reality: Anekāntavāda affirms that reality has many aspects and that finite statements are partial, but it does not claim that any interpretation is acceptable. Standpoints must be grounded in valid pramāṇa and constrained by logical and ethical criteria. Jain philosophers explicitly criticize dogmatic claims that exceed available evidence, while also rejecting a nihilistic relativism that ignores the difference between well-supported and poorly supported views.

misconceptions.myth: Syādvāda is just a rhetorical device to avoid taking a clear position on doctrinal or ethical issues.
misconceptions.reality: Syādvāda is a rigorous logical and linguistic discipline that marks how far one’s evidence extends and which aspect of reality is being described. By using conditional qualifiers—“in some respect,” “from a certain standpoint”—it allows precise, context-sensitive assertions rather than vague indecision. This helps Jains articulate firm ethical commitments, such as ahiṃsā, while acknowledging complexity in how those commitments are applied in diverse situations.

misconceptions.myth: Because Jainism recognizes extrasensory and omniscient knowledge, ordinary empirical evidence is considered unimportant or unreliable.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts carefully classify empirical and inferential knowledge as valid but indirect pramāṇa. These forms of evidence are indispensable for everyday life and for much philosophical reasoning. Higher forms of knowledge do not negate empirical evidence; they refine and sometimes correct it, showing its limits. The hierarchy of pramāṇas is meant to integrate, not dismiss, ordinary cognition within a broader path toward clearer, less obstructed knowing.
